pages.text: The Frozen Poles

image.note: Cover: an icy polar landscape, a bear one side, a penguin the other

pages.text: Contents. A World of Ice / The Frozen North / The Frozen South / Life in the Cold / The Poles and the World / The Ends of the Earth.

At the very top of the world, and at the very bottom, lie two places colder than anywhere else on earth: the frozen poles. Here the ice never melts, the winters are dark for months, and only the toughest creatures survive. Few people ever go there. This is the story of the ends of the earth, and the astonishing life that clings to them.

image.note: The globe with both frozen poles marked

pages.text: The two poles seem alike, both white, both frozen, both ruled by ice and cold. But they are, in truth, opposites, and one of the strangest facts about them is this: the two most famous polar animals of all, the polar bear and the penguin, live at opposite ends of the earth, and have never once met.

image.note: A polar bear at the top, a penguin at the bottom, apart

pages.text: Why are the poles so cold? Because of the Sun, or rather, the lack of it. The earth is tilted, and at the poles the Sun never climbs high in the sky. Its light strikes at a low, weak slant, spreading thin across the ice, and never warming it. Even in summer, the poles stay frozen.

image.note: The Sun's weak, slanting light at the pole

pages.text: The tilt does something else strange. For part of the year the pole leans so far from the Sun that it does not rise at all, and the darkness lasts for weeks or months: the long polar night. Then the year turns, and the Sun does not set, and it is daylight around the clock: the midnight sun. Imagine a day that lasts for months, and a night just as long.

image.note: The midnight sun circling above the ice

pages.text: The pole at the top of the world is called the Arctic. And here is its great secret: the Arctic is not land at all. It is a vast, frozen ocean, a lid of thick ice floating on the cold sea, ringed by the northern edges of Europe, Asia, and North America.

image.note: The Arctic as a frozen sea ringed by land

pages.text: Life clings on, even here. Beneath the ice swim fish and seals; upon it prowls the great white polar bear, the mighty hunter of the north, at home on the frozen sea. Whales rise at cracks in the ice to breathe. The Arctic looks empty, but it teems with tough and clever life.

image.note: A polar bear prowling the Arctic ice

pages.text: And people live in the Arctic too, and have for thousands of years. The Inuit and other northern peoples learned long ago to survive the fierce cold, to hunt and fish and shelter, and to thrive where almost no one else could. The frozen north is harsh, but it has long been home.

image.note: Inuit people living in the Arctic

pages.text: Now travel to the bottom of the world, to the opposite pole, and you find the opposite thing. Here the pole is not frozen sea but frozen land: a whole continent, Antarctica, buried under ice so deep it could swallow mountains, ringed all around by the stormy southern ocean.

image.note: Antarctica as a vast frozen continent

pages.text: Antarctica is the coldest, windiest, emptiest place on all the earth. No towns, no farms, no people who truly live there. Only visiting scientists, in snug research stations, come to study its ice and its secrets, before returning home. It is the last great wilderness, kept for science and for wonder.

image.note: A research station on the Antarctic ice

pages.text: Yet even here, life finds a way, around the frozen edges. Penguins throng the icy shores in their thousands, waddling and swimming and huddling against the cold. Seals bask on the ice, and whales feed in the rich cold sea. And penguins, remember, live only here, in the south, never in the north with the bears.

image.note: A great colony of penguins on the Antarctic shore

pages.text: How does anything survive such cold? Every polar animal has its own clever answer. Many wear thick fur or dense feathers, trapping warmth like the cosiest coat. Beneath the skin, most carry a thick layer of fat, called blubber, that holds in heat like a blanket wrapped from within.

image.note: A cross-section showing blubber keeping an animal warm

pages.text: They help each other, too. Penguins huddle together in great crowds against the wind, each sheltering the next, taking turns to stand at the cold outer edge. Many polar animals are white, to hide against the snow, whether to sneak up on food or to keep from becoming it. In the cold, cleverness is survival.

image.note: Penguins huddling together against the wind

pages.text: The frozen poles may seem far away and empty, but they matter to the whole world. Their vast white ice reflects the Sun's heat back into space, helping to keep the whole earth cool. Locked in that ice is a huge share of all the fresh water on the planet. The poles help keep the balance of the world.

image.note: The white poles reflecting sunlight back into space

pages.text: Scientists watch the poles closely, for the ice tells the story of our planet's health. As the world slowly warms, the polar ice is one of the places where the change shows first. What happens at the frozen ends of the earth matters to every land between them, including your own.

So there they lie, at the top and bottom of our spinning world: two frozen poles, opposite in almost every way. A frozen ocean in the north, where bears hunt and people have long lived. A frozen continent in the south, where penguins throng and only scientists visit. Two white wildernesses, colder than anywhere else on earth.

image.note: Both poles side by side, north and south

pages.text: They are the hardest places on earth to live, and among the most beautiful. Few of us will ever stand upon their ice or watch their endless day. But now you know their secret: two poles, alike and opposite, ruled by cold and dark and dazzling light, at the very ends of our extraordinary world.

image.note: A lone figure beneath the vast polar sky

pages.text: Words to know. The Arctic: the frozen ocean at the top of the world. Antarctica: the frozen continent at the bottom. Blubber: the thick fat that keeps polar animals warm. Midnight sun: when the Sun never sets. Polar night: when the Sun never rises.

image.note: Labelled map of the two poles

pages.text: The poles are frozen, but not lifeless, and they help hold the whole world in balance. From the coldest ice to the warmest river, our planet is full of astonishing places. Which will you explore next?

image.note: The frozen poles beside a warm river
